attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter, stated in his voice with "To be explicit".

semantics.note: An unhedged present-tense claim covering two categories: AI software and AI add-ons. Adding "real" in the normalised wording is a slight gloss, but it fits the context, which says demand barely exists without hyperscaler money.

contract.note: Read literally, "not there" is defeated by any paid buyers, yet the speaker himself mentions paid seats. Reading it as demand too weak to justify the investment is an ordinary, fair plain reading. Choosing the April–June quarter is the evaluator's call, not the speaker's, and the result depends on how adequacy is judged.

evidence.note: Microsoft's own report for the quarter ending June 30: over 30M paid Copilot seats and large deployments. This cuts against a literal reading. It gives no prices, discounts, renewals or returns, and the contract says seat counts alone do not settle the claim.

An independent measure of June 2026 business spending, but only vendor-level adoption of OpenAI and Anthropic. It does not separate software from model services or link spending to costs and investment.
IMF note published Oct 9, before the evaluation date. It finds circular financing across the AI sector, but does not show that software demand in April–June was insufficient or depended on financing.

reviews.rationale: Zitron's claim is an unhedged observation, and the contract's adequacy reading is fair. The packet doesn't settle it either way. Microsoft's paid-seat figures are its own disclosure and, under the contract, cannot alone contradict the claim. Ramp's data does not separate software from model services. The IMF note gives sector-wide financing context only. Nothing in the packet ties customer payments or renewals in either category to costs and investment, so neither the support nor the contradiction condition is met.
